/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
out = Path('tmp/pdfs')
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
pages = []
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages, 1):
    content = page.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    pages.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n{content}')
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(pages))
print('Pages:', len(reader.pages))
print('Metadata:', reader.metadata)
print('\\n'.join(pages[:3]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re, statistics
text = Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').read_text()
p13 = text.split('===== PAGE 13 =====')[1].split('===== PAGE 14 =====')[0]
rows=[]
for line in p13.splitlines():
    match = re.match(r'"'^'"\\s*([a-z ]+?)\\s{2,}(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)',line)
    if match:
        rows.append((match.group(1).strip(), *map(float, match.groups()[1:])))
print('Occupation rows:', len(rows))
for label, group in [('male-stereotyped', rows[:20]), ('female-stereotyped', rows[20:]), ('all', rows)]:
    print(label, 'single STS', statistics.mean(r[1] for r in group), 'paired STS', statistics.mean(r[3] for r in group), 'single %F', statistics.mean(r[2] for r in group))
print('Mean absolute micro STS: single', statistics.mean(abs(r[1]) for r in rows), 'paired', statistics.mean(abs(r[3]) for r in rows))
p15 = text.split('===== PAGE 15 =====')[1]
power=[]
for line in p15.splitlines():
    match=re.match(r'"'^'"\\s*([a-z ]+?)\\s{2,}(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)',line)
    if match: power.append((match.group(1).strip(), *map(float, match.groups()[1:])))
print('Power rows:',len(power))
for label, group in [('powerful', [r for r in power if r[0].endswith('power')]), ('powerless', [r for r in power if r[0].endswith('minor')]), ('all',power)]:
    print(label,'single STS',statistics.mean(r[1] for r in group),'paired STS',statistics.mean(r[2] for r in group))
PY"

strengths: PST addresses a relevant gap in multimodal NLP evaluation: gender associations when multiple people are generated together. The distinction between occupational stereotypes and organizational power provides a useful research direction.

The occupational experiment covers all 400 cross-group occupation pairs and reverses their positions, producing 800 images. The substantial observed stereotype conformity supports the narrower conclusion that these paired prompts elicit occupational stereotypes in the tested DALL-E-3 system.

Three human annotators per target and reported Fleiss’ kappa values of 0.88–0.92 support annotation consistency. Testing BLIP against human judgments usefully demonstrates why that automated classifier is unsuitable for this paired setting.

The paper clearly explains the basic protocol and supplies occupation lists, prompt templates, annotation instructions, and detailed results. These materials make the proposed evaluation understandable and facilitate reimplementation.
weaknesses: The interpretation of STS does not match the stated fairness criterion. STS measures signed stereotype conformity, whereas Section 3.1 defines fairness through equal gender probabilities for each identity. Opposing imbalances can cancel: Table 3 averages single-person scores of -30 and +50 into an overall score of 10. Consequently, higher paired STS establishes stronger stereotype conformity, not necessarily greater overall unfairness. Claims of unbiased single-person generation and uniformly preferable lower STS require revision, with per-identity parity deviations reported separately.

Statistical support is inadequate for several detailed conclusions. The baseline uses only three images per identity, while paired occupational generation has one sample per ordered pair. No confidence intervals or statistical tests accompany occupation rankings, reversals, mitigation effects, or the small powerful-versus-powerless difference. The aggregate occupational shift is substantial, but these finer claims require more sampling and uncertainty estimates that account for the paired observations.

The organizational-power comparison does not establish matched role descriptors across conditions. Figure 6, for example, shows leader/employee for the single-person developer examples but manager/assistant for the paired example. Changes in role wording can therefore contribute to the measured difference. Exact matching across conditions and replication across role choices are needed to attribute changes confidently to paired generation.

Measurement validity is incompletely documented. Table 10 permits 'Cannot Identify,' but its treatment in the binary metric and the aggregation of three annotators’ responses are unspecified. There is also no reported audit of whether generated people actually satisfy the requested occupations and positional assignments. Agreement on perceived gender traits does not establish correct role binding.

Reproducibility remains insufficient despite the useful appendices. The generation interface, dates/settings, exact occupation–power combinations, and handling of any prompt rewriting are undocumented; no generated-image archive, annotation release, or implementation is identified. These omissions matter for auditing results from a changing proprietary system.

The mitigation evidence is preliminary: occupational evaluation selects the most biased occupations, without a clearly documented fresh unchanged-prompt control or uncertainty analysis. Selection effects and regression to the mean are therefore unresolved, and aggregate signed-score reductions do not establish improved fairness for individual roles. Together with the metric, comparison, and reproducibility concerns, this warrants substantive revisions before a Findings recommendation.
